M4 · Transformer Equivalent Circuit (Ch3)

Why this matters in the exam: Q2 of every exam is “Magnetic Circuits and Transformers” (20 marks). About half of it is this pack. Jun23 Q2b (5 marks) was OC/SC test parameters and Q2c (6 marks) was writing from the simplified circuit and explaining its phase. Jun24 Q2b (5 marks) was ideal-transformer impedance referral. The 2023 quiz (Q6, 9 marks) and the 2024 test (Q6–Q8, 12 marks) used the same skills. Expect 10–12 of the 20 Q2 marks to need exactly these methods.

Scope: ideal transformer, referred quantities, full and simplified equivalent circuits, OC and SC tests, and finding or from the circuit. Regulation, efficiency and 3-phase transformer analysis are in pack M5. The only 3-phase skill used here is converting test readings to per-phase values.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Ideal transformer (Lecture 3.7.5–3.7.8)

The course defines the turns ratio as and writes a transformer as “”. The ideal case assumes zero leakage flux and zero core reluctance.

Relationship Formula When to use Common trap

Current ratio Same Current goes the opposite way to voltage
Power , so , Checking answers Holds only for the ideal transformer
Input impedance Seeing a load “through” the transformer It is , not

1.2 Referred quantities (Lecture 3.8.1)

“Referring to the primary” removes the transformer from the circuit. Referred quantities carry a prime:

  • Use it whenever a circuit has impedances on both sides. Redraw everything on the primary side. Solve an ordinary series/parallel circuit. Convert back with and .
  • Referring the other way (primary impedance to the secondary) divides by .
  • Trap: the phase angles do not change when you refer. Only the magnitudes scale.

1.3 The four non-idealities and their circuit elements (Lecture 3.9.1–3.9.2)

Non-ideality Element Position Effect
Finite core permeability (magnetising reactance) shunt Magnetising current flows even at no load, so
Iron loss (hysteresis + eddy) (core-loss resistance) shunt Loss , roughly constant at fixed voltage
Leakage flux , series Output voltage falls as load current rises
Winding resistance , series Copper loss

models core loss as a resistor because (back-emf equation) and core loss , which is how a resistor behaves (Practice 3.26b).

1.5 The two tests (Lecture 3.10.2–3.10.4)

Open-circuit (OC) test Short-circuit (SC) test
Set-up Secondary open, rated voltage on primary Secondary shorted, reduced voltage (about 10% of rated) to get about rated current
What remains of the circuit (parallel) (series)
Why the rest is neglected , and is small, so the series drop is tiny is small, so the shunt currents () are tiny
Formulas , ,
Common to both , same
Typical size pu pu

The key rule: parallel elements use . Series elements use .

3-phase (star): convert first. , , . Then use the single-phase formulas. The parameters you get are per phase.

Side matters: the parameters come out referred to the side you energised. If the OC test is done on the LV side (common in practice), multiply and by to refer them to the HV primary.

Example 3: Real OC data and saturation (your Prac 2)

Given: your Prac 2 transformer is 240/120 V, 1 kVA. OC tests on the 240 V winding gave:

Nominal (V) (A) (W)
100 V 102.67 0.04 3.14
170 V 172.35 0.10 8.83
240 V 239.75 0.66 20.12

Find: and at each voltage using the lecture method. Explain the trend.

Solution

Use , , , . The current components are and .

(V) (VA) (VAr) pf (Ω) (Ω) (A) (A)
102.67 4.107 2.647 0.765 3357 3982 0.031 0.026
172.35 17.24 14.80 0.512 3364 2007 0.051 0.086
239.75 158.2 157.0 0.127 2857 366.2 0.084 0.655

Reading it:

  • falls from 3982 Ω to 366 Ω, a 91% drop. The voltage went up by a factor of only 2.3.
  • From the back-emf equation, . At 240 V the core is past the knee of the B–H curve. The incremental permeability drops, so the reluctance rises, falls, and falls (from 12.7 H to 1.17 H).
  • The magnetising current shows it directly. If had stayed at 3982 Ω, then at 240 V would be 0.060 A. The measured value was 0.655 A, about 11 times larger, and the current waveform was visibly distorted.
  • moves much less (3357 → 2857 Ω). Core loss depends on and , not on permeability, so still roughly holds.
  • The pf drops from 0.77 to 0.13. At rated voltage the OC current is almost purely magnetising.

Exam lesson: the equivalent circuit parameters are valid only at the voltage where you measured them. That is why the OC test is done at rated voltage. The 240 V row (366 Ω) is the one to use for rated operation.

Lecture method vs prac method: your VI used the “exact” method from the handout. It subtracts the drop across first (, with Ω and Ω), which gives Ω and Ω (the VI printed 2865 and 366.09 Ω). The lecture method above gives 2857 and 366.2 Ω, within 0.3%. In the exam, use the lecture method () unless the question says otherwise.

One caution: A was recorded to 2 d.p. Anything from 0.035 to 0.045 A would give between 6030 Ω and 3110 Ω at 100 V. So the low-voltage values are uncertain, but the 91% collapse is far bigger than that uncertainty.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • SC/OC formulas swapped. The OC test is parallel (, ). The SC test is series (, ). If your comes out at 0.6 Ω, you have swapped them.
  • Using for . In the SC test , not . In the OC test is the parallel combination, not . You need from .
  • Forgetting the per-phase conversion for a star 3-phase test: and . Getting it wrong puts out by a factor of 3 and by a factor of or 3.
  • Not referring secondary parameters. Practice 3.27 says “secondary parameters are NOT referred”. , not .
  • OC test done on the LV side. The resulting , are referred to the LV side. Multiply by before putting them on an HV-primary circuit.
  • Putting and into the KVL. In the simplified circuit they hang across . They carry no and do not affect .
  • Wrong sign on the current angle. Lagging pf (load absorbs Q) means . A load “generating” Q is leading, so (2024 test Q7).
  • “Capacitive load makes lead”. A capacitive load raises , but still lags for any normal load (see New Question 4). Don’t confuse a magnitude rise with a phase lead.

2024 test Q8 (4 marks). Short-Answer Question. Answer the following question using words only (that is, without using sketches or equations).

Consider an ideal transformer driving a resistive load of resistance . Carefully explain what would be the effect on the output voltage and current if the load resistance was doubled. Carefully explain why and how this would be different for a real transformer.

Solution
  • Ideal transformer. The output voltage stays constant, because it is set only by the input voltage and the turns ratio and is not affected by the load current. The output current halves, by Ohm’s law, because the load resistance has doubled.
  • Real transformer. It has series winding resistance and leakage reactance. When the load current falls, the voltage drop across these series terms falls, so the output voltage rises slightly. The output current therefore falls to slightly more than half of its original value.

(Exam instruction: words only, so no equations or sketches.) These are the course’s model points.

New Question 5 (hard, saturation) [5 marks]. A single-phase 240 V, 50 Hz transformer has two OC tests on its primary:

  • at 120 V: 0.050 A, 2.2 W
  • at 240 V: 0.42 A, 8.6 W
  1. Find and at both voltages. [2]
  2. A designer uses only the 120 V values to predict the no-load current and iron loss at 240 V. What do they predict, and how does that compare with the measurement? [2]
  3. Explain the difference in one or two sentences, and say which values belong in the equivalent circuit for rated operation. [1]
Solution
  1. 120 V: VA, VAr. . .

240 V: VA, VAr. . .

  1. Predicted: A and A, so A. W.

Measured: 0.42 A and 8.6 W. The loss prediction is good (within 2%), but the current is about 4 times too low.

  1. At 240 V the peak flux density is twice as high (back-emf equation), and the core is in saturation. The permeability falls, so falls from 8.2 H to 1.8 H and the magnetising current rises sharply. Core loss still scales as , so stays roughly constant. Use the rated-voltage (240 V) values. This is the same effect as your Prac 2.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

TRANSFORMER EQUIVALENT CIRCUIT (Ch3)                    n = N1/N2 (rated V1/V2)
Ideal:    V1 = nV2   I1 = I2/n   ZIN = n^2 ZL   S1 = S2
Refer to primary:  V2' = nV2   I2' = I2/n   Z' = n^2 Z   (angles unchanged)
          back:     V2 = V2'/n   I2 = n I2'
Simplified circuit (ref. to primary): RC || jXM across V1, then R + jX series to V2'
          R = R1 + R2' = R1 + n^2 R2      X = X1 + X2' = X1 + n^2 X2
TESTS (3ph star: V = VL/sqrt3, I = IL, P = Ptot/3 FIRST)   S = VI, Q = sqrt(S^2 - P^2)
  OC (rated V, sec open)  -> PARALLEL:  RC = V^2/P    XM = V^2/Q
  SC (low V, sec shorted) -> SERIES:    R  = P/I^2    X  = Q/I^2     (check |Z| = V/I)
  Params come out on the side you energised -> x n^2 to move LV -> HV
USING IT
  KVL:      V2' = V1 - I2'(R + jX)        V1 = V2' + I2'(R + jX)
  Divider:  V2' = V1 * ZL'/(ZL' + R + jX)
  I1 = I2' + V1/RC + V1/(jXM)
  Output conditions: V2' = V1rated(phase) <0 ;  I2' = S/V2' (1ph) or S/(sqrt3 VL) (3ph)
     angle phi = -acos(pf) lagging (absorbs Q), +acos(pf) leading (generates Q)
  Phase: resistive (or capacitive) load -> V2' LAGS V1 (series X makes I2' lag; V2' in phase with I2')
Reverse: no-load |I| = sqrt((V/RC)^2 + (V/XM)^2), P = V^2/RC ; SC: |I| = V/|R+jX|, P = I^2 R
Saturation: XM valid only at the test voltage (Prac 2: 3982 -> 366 ohm from 100 -> 240 V). Use the rated-V OC test.
